title: Hanyu Pinyin at 60: What Drove the Latinization of Chinese Characters, and Why Did Our Thinking Change?
excerpt: All of this has to start with one question: how to get every Chinese person onto a computer.
body:
All of this has to start with one question: how to get every Chinese person onto a computer.

Suppose someone was born in southern China in 1964 — a man, let's say. In first grade he learned Hanyu Pinyin, and through it the sounds of Mandarin. For the next 30 years he very likely had no occasion to use pinyin again. Then came the 1990s.

He was assigned to a new post, and what troubled him was not the new technology but the new terms in the paperwork. Drafting a document, he did not know how to write them. A colleague told him, for instance, that 混凝土, the word for concrete, had been shortened to a single character pronounced tóng.

On the office's shared computer, he tapped out the four letters t-o-n-g one key at a time. After hunting through the list, he found it: 砼.

Pinyin was not part of daily life then. Probably not until his children bought him his first computer did this member of the "post-60s" generation have to dig the rules of pinyin back out of memory. And not until he got his first smart device with handwriting input did he stop racking his brain over how characters were pronounced — he went back to writing characters directly, though he still struggled to tell front nasals from back nasals, and retroflex initials from plain ones.

For his children and grandchildren, pinyin is something else entirely. For the youngest generation especially, it is so ordinary that there is a word — "hand cancer" — for the typos you make in a hurry.

February 11, 2018 marked the 60th anniversary of Hanyu Pinyin. It was created to be "a tool for annotating the sound of Chinese characters and for promoting Mandarin." With the spread of personal computers and smart devices, it has become the dominant way people talk in the virtual world.

The most recent crisis for Chinese characters came in the 1970s. In the computer's first years, making Chinese fit the machine was an urgent problem. [Wang Yongmin, the inventor of the Wubi input method, put it this way](https://wenku.baidu.com/view/ef2b5a05b52acfc789ebc9f7.html): "When the computer arrived in China, Chinese and foreigners alike shared one great puzzle — could tens of thousands of Chinese characters fit into a computer with only 26 letter keys? In those years, newspapers at home and abroad ran articles calling the computer 'the gravedigger of Chinese characters and the midwife of phonetic script,' proclaiming that Chinese characters had 'walked into a dead end of the times' and should 'meet their natural end.'"

Wubi rescued the situation, then quickly gave way to pinyin, which has ruled ever since — and its significance goes well beyond being the dominant input method. If pen and paper play little part in your life, you will find that the way you put words down has become entirely Latinized. That is truer every year.

In other words, for the person doing the writing, China's ideographic script has already given way to an environment of Latin-alphabet pinyin. What the scholars who once opposed reforming Chinese characters feared seems to be coming true.

All of this has to start with one question: how to get every Chinese person onto a computer.

### 1. Why Did Wubi Take Hold Before Pinyin?

Wang Yongmin, a researcher on Chinese-character proofreading and phototypesetting machines, spent five years on Wubi and released it in 1983. The method breaks a character down by shape and pairs its components with the Latin letters on the keyboard; three letters produce one specific character. State backing followed — both the State Science and Technology Commission and the Commission of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense issued documents calling for Wubi's promotion — and Wubi became the first Chinese input method a whole generation learned. Many people signed up for computer classes where one lesson was Wubi drills; they had to learn the chart taped beside the keyboard that mapped character components to keys.

[Wang Yongmin later published an article in *Qiushi* magazine](https://wenku.baidu.com/view/ef2b5a05b52acfc789ebc9f7.html) recalling how he invented it: "Chinese has only a little over 400 syllables, which have to cover tens of thousands of characters. With pinyin input, it is 'easy to type, hard to find the character.'" Duplicate codes were indeed widely regarded as the biggest weakness of early pinyin input.

![Wang Yongmin](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180221152910TSVWKDFrp3MYhCZ1.jpg-w600)

Looked at from the characters' side, only two features tell one from another: sound and shape. Pinyin could not improve input speed at the time. And going at the problem through shape had a second, more intuitive appeal: typing a character this way felt like writing it, which seemed closer to how Chinese people were used to putting words on paper.

"Xu Shen, the philologist of our Eastern Han dynasty, pointed to the way through nearly 1,900 years ago. In *Shuowen Jiezi*, he analyzed Chinese characters as a whole and revealed the inner logic of their construction: 'A single-component form is called wen; a compound form is called zi.' He held that the tens of thousands of Chinese characters are all assembled, like building blocks, from some 500 basic single-component forms. These basic forms are called 'wen'; what you build by combining 'wen' is called 'zi.' There are only a few hundred 'wen,' but there can be tens of thousands of 'zi,'" [Wang Yongmin recalled in a speech.](http://www.wangma.com.cn/wym_disp.asp?id=44)

Wang was not, however, the first to input characters by taking their shapes apart. In 1976 Zhu Bangfu, based in Taiwan, published his shape-and-meaning retrieval method; two years later Chiang Wei-kuo named it after Cangjie, the court official credited in Chinese legend with inventing writing — hence the Cangjie input method.

Zhu Bangfu was born in 1937 in Huanggang, Hubei. The wars moved him and his father to Taiwan; he later spent time in Brazil, the United States and elsewhere, and returned to Taiwan in 1973. Zhu said he had always wanted to input characters through their shapes: "Because in my years of research I found the basic elements of writing: for input, character codes; for sorting, letters; for recognition, basic shapes and positions; and character shapes can be composed from the proportions of their strokes."

Another shape-based method popular in the 1990s was Zhengma, started by Zheng Yili, a Chinese philologist and the editor-in-chief of the *English-Chinese Dictionary*《英华大词典》, and finished by his daughter Zheng Long. Zhengma was patented in 1989 and was later built into Microsoft Windows as one of its bundled input methods.

"Early pinyin input methods were not very successful, and that created the conditions for other methods to rise fast," the natural-language-processing expert Wu Jun wrote in his book *The Beauty of Mathematics*《数学之美》. "By the early 1990s there were already more than a thousand patents on input methods — so many that some experts believed the reason China's software industry could not get ahead was that everyone had gone off to build input methods."

Specialist input methods flooded the market, and the most successful was of course Wubi. Every company then had a job title stamped with its era: the Wubi typist, whose work was turning handwritten documents into electronic files.

![A chart of Wubi character components and their keys](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180221153101W46oR8TPhylZpdNx.jpeg-w600)

Wu Jun argued that Wubi won not because Wubi itself was so good. Analyzing the problem through the mathematics of information theory, he concluded that three keystrokes were, in principle, all it took to produce one character. "Wang Yongmin's Wubi won for the time being not because his method was more rational, but because he was better at marketing than the other inventors."

Wu went further: complex methods like Wubi carry a built-in flaw. He cited experiments showing that people using them typed, when composing freely, at a quarter of the speed they managed when copying from a written text. "These methods make you take characters apart on the spot according to rules. That not only takes time, it badly interrupts the train of thought when you are composing freely… which is why the great majority of Chinese computer users think very little of this class of input method."

Getting from beginner to 80 or 90 characters a minute in Wubi took about two months. And unless you were typing from a finished manuscript, it was easy to slip back into pinyin. That seems to bear out Wu Jun's point: thought usually runs in sound. Mapping thought onto character shapes and then feeding those shapes into a computer is not an intuitive process.

### 2. What Actually Kept Pinyin From Becoming the Mainstream Input Method?

The answer is memory.

Smart ABC, released in 1995, counts as the easiest pinyin input method of its early years, and it was still clumsy. You typed the pinyin, hit the space bar, and a huge bank of characters appeared. Its word-frequency presets were poor, so users spent a long time hunting for the one they wanted. Syllables like shi and zhi, which cover a great many characters, were maddening. So many people at the time typed two-character words instead: to get 雅虎, the Chinese name for Yahoo, they would call up 典雅 ("refined") and 老虎 ("tiger") and then delete the characters they did not want — still not an efficient way to type.

In December 1999 Ziguang Pinyin, grown out of an earlier product called Kaola Pinyin, was formally released. Ziguang put 雅虎 straight into its built-in dictionary: type yahu and the word came up.

Winning efficiency through a dictionary, the way Ziguang did, required more storage. By 1999 a mainstream computer had 64MB of memory and a 6.4GB hard drive. That is what made Ziguang Pinyin possible. Pinyin methods kept updating after that, adding fuzzy pinyin (to help people with regional accents use pinyin) and custom dictionaries (so the method remembers in advance the characters and words a particular user reaches for), and pinyin got faster still.

Look back to the start: the 1981 IBM PC had just 4KB of memory, and permanent storage meant 5.25-inch floppy disks holding at most 1.2MB each. With so little room to work in, using a Chinese input method meant plugging in a so-called hanka, a "Chinese character card" — a read-only memory unit carrying a Chinese input program.

In 1989 Shi Yuzhu built the M-6401 desktop word-processing system and packed it into a read-only memory unit. Through that piece of add-on hardware, the hanka let the computers of the day take Chinese characters in and put them out. On the hanka alone, Shi Yuzhu's revenue passed 1 million yuan in four months. Most of China's earliest technology companies were in the hanka business at one point, Lenovo and Founder among them, and so was Wang Yongmin's Wangma Group.

![Giant Group's M-6403 hanka card](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180221153307m5seYA0QUDWJoqxi.jpeg-w600)

These advances, hidden in code, chips and electronic components, are unfamiliar to most users now. As hardware improved, all of it was folded into the operating system, and the hanka was retired long ago. Still, the hanka can be read as the input method's ancestor. At bottom the two were solving the same problem: how to let an ordinary person use a computer. The hanka, being hardware, was eliminated; the programs inside it, the input method above all, kept evolving and updating.

### 3. Wang Xuan, the Bi Sheng of Our Time

Making Chinese characters and computers compatible was a "systems engineering" problem with several sides, input and output among them. If the Chinese input methods that arrived one after another in the late 1970s solved input, then Wang Xuan and the laser phototypesetting he invented solved output. In that sense, calling Wang Xuan the Bi Sheng of our time is no exaggeration.

Traditional Chinese printing still ran on lead type, and it was slow. One unverified story has it that Zhu Bangfu, working at a Brazilian publishing house, found that an English book could be typeset, proofread and printed by computer in as little as 12 hours, while a Chinese book — set and proofread in lead before it went to press — took half a year from start to finish. Chinese-language information moved extremely slowly, and in an age of exploding knowledge that was a serious threat.

The biggest difference between Chinese and English printing still came down to the characters. English printing needed 26 letters and a handful of punctuation marks; Chinese depended on tens of thousands of characters. As with input methods, the obstacle was that a 512KB storage device could not hold that much.

Wang Xuan's approach had something in common with Zhu Bangfu's Cangjie and Wang Yongmin's Wubi. By analyzing character shapes, he split them into regular strokes and irregular ones — the first could be expressed as parameters, the second described by outlines — which amounted to encoding characters in a simpler way, without having to store the full shape of each one. The new codes took 1/500 of the original space. Add the faster output speeds, and Wang Xuan's laser phototypesetting solved the printing of Chinese characters in the electronic age.

### 4. The Rise of Pinyin Input

The phone's evolution deserves much of the credit for pinyin's mass adoption.

[According to a 2006 report in the *Shanghai Youth Daily*](http://news.sohu.com/20061107/n246239201.shtml): "Because the mobile-phone market was basically held by international giants like Nokia, Motorola and Samsung, whose input methods followed standards such as America's T9 and Canada's 'Ziyuan' — T9 alone holding about 50 percent of the market — this directly shaped what the whole mobile-phone market wanted from Chinese input."

T9 is what is usually called the nine-key keypad. Before it, typing on a phone meant pressing a key over and over: to enter the letter B you pressed the 2 key twice in a row. The nine-key simplification was that you pressed the key the letter sits on once, and an algorithm assembled a valid pinyin syllable, which made Chinese input faster. Together with the text-message boom — 300 billion SMS messages were sent nationwide in 2005 — T9 quickly carried pinyin along with it.

Soon after, the smartphone put a full computer keyboard on the phone screen. Phone and computer input converged: learn one pinyin input method and you could type anywhere without friction.

Sogou Pinyin launched in 2006. Sogou CTO Yang Hongtao recalls that in the 1990s an input method's dictionary came from counting word frequencies across the mass of reporting printed in the official newspapers of the day. The dictionary that produced matched neither how users actually spoke nor how fast society was changing, so a user typing pinyin still had to spend time picking a word out of the list, and accuracy improved only so much.

Sogou's rise was built on exactly this demand for speed. The principle, put simply: Sogou Pinyin used the company's search technology to push its dictionary to the limit — the entire Chinese-language internet. By matching what a user typed against all of it, it could pick out what that user most likely meant.

Yang Hongtao likes one example. 2006 was the year *Super Girl* was at its hottest. By crawling the web, Sogou made it possible to type liyuchun and have the singer Li Yuchun's name suggested whole, instead of entering the three characters of it one at a time. Stretching the dictionary to the size of the Chinese internet brought Sogou Pinyin close to Wu Jun's ideal scheme: "Given a language model of unlimited size, you can reach the input speed limit that information theory sets."

Sogou Pinyin quickly became the most mainstream input method on the market, its share passing 90 percent within a year. Only when Google, Tencent and Baidu each built their own internet-based Chinese input methods did that share slide, and it never fell below 70 percent.

![Sogou Pinyin](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180221153739Tg0XQFGky7W3dORv.jpeg-w600)

### 5. Now We Can Go Back to the History of Latinizing Chinese Characters

Jesuit missionaries who came to China to preach as early as the Ming dynasty tried using Latin letters to mark the sound of Chinese characters, to ease exchange between East and West. By the end of the 19th century, editions of the Bible using Latin letters to transcribe the local dialect had appeared all over the country. Western missionaries were the first practitioners of Latinized Chinese.

The first person to argue outright for Latinizing Chinese characters was Song Shu, a student of the late-Qing classicist Yu Yue. In *Humble Remarks from the Six Studios*《六斋卑议》 he wrote: "South of the Jianghuai region, several kinds of phonetic script must be created, for the sake of elementary schooling." Song Shu, in other words, thought Chinese characters were too complex and too hard to learn next to a phonetic script, which kept illiteracy high and held back the country's social progress and development.

The New Culture Movement, from 1915 on, largely inherited the idea, and the calls and slogans for abolishing Chinese characters grew fiercer. Qu Qiubai demanded: "The new Chinese writing of modern Mandarin must be Romanized — switched to the Roman alphabet — and Chinese characters must be abolished root and branch." Cai Yuanpei held that "since Chinese characters cannot avoid reform, we may as well switch straight to the Latin alphabet." Lu Xun went so far as to cry: "If Chinese characters are not destroyed, China will perish."

In 1918 the Republic of China's Ministry of Education formally introduced the Zhuyin system. It can be read as an early form of Hanyu Pinyin; the big difference is that Zhuyin was based on the "niuwen" and "yunwen" systems invented by Zhang Taiyan rather than on familiar Latin letters like a, b, c, d. Zhuyin went through many revisions and is now used mainly in Taiwan. The mainland replaced it with Hanyu Pinyin after 1958, but reference works such as the *Xinhua Dictionary* and the *Contemporary Chinese Dictionary* still keep Zhuyin spellings.

The Chinese Communist Party carried the Latinization tradition on for a long stretch. After the October Revolution the Soviet Union launched a movement to Latinize scripts and set up a committee to study Latinizing Chinese, aiming to make illiterate workers in northern China literate so that they could become a backbone of the international communist movement.

In February 1929 Qu Qiubai drew up the first scheme for Latinized Chinese, and in October he wrote a pamphlet, *The Latinized Chinese Alphabet*《中国拉丁化字母》. After the Soviet Union helped revise it, the scheme was formally promoted from 1934 in areas the Communists held and in regions under heavy Soviet influence. The linguist Chen Ping notes in *Modern Chinese*《现代汉语》 that from 1933 until the scheme was abolished in 1944, more than 300 publications — about 500,000 copies — used this Latinized new script.

![Dazhong Bao, printed in the Latinized script](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180221153829U2LBWIT9j7frVyde.jpg-w600)

The policy continued after 1949. Having watched Mongolia, Vietnam, North Korea and others convert their scripts to Latin alphabets, Liu Shaoqi asked the Central Propaganda Department to study those countries' experience of script reform as a reference for China's own plan. Mao Zedong likewise held that "writing must be reformed, and must move toward the phonetic direction common to the world's scripts."

There was no shortage of opposition. The archaeologist and oracle-bone scholar Chen Mengjia was the earliest and best known dissenter. In 1957 he published *Be a Little More Careful About "Reforming" Chinese Characters* and *On the Future of Chinese Characters*, opposing both the replacement of traditional characters with simplified ones and the Latinization of Chinese. Given the politics of the time, Chen Mengjia was soon branded a rightist, and he killed himself during the Cultural Revolution.

In the end the Party settled on a compromise. In *Oracle Bones*, Peter Hessler quotes Zhou Youguang's view that it was Stalin who changed Mao's mind.

"At that time Mao respected Stalin greatly and treated him as the leader of the communist world. He told Stalin that China was going to carry out a script reform, and asked what he thought. Stalin told him: 'You are a great nation. You should have your own, Chinese-style writing. You should not simply use the Latin alphabet.'"

The Party did give up the idea of Latinizing Chinese characters completely. In 1958 the linguist Zhou Youguang and his team invented Hanyu Pinyin — more than 20 years before the first real personal computer, the IBM PC of 1981.

That same year, in *The Current Tasks of Script Reform*《当前文字改革的任务》, Zhou Enlai wrote: "First, it should be made clear that the Hanyu Pinyin scheme is for annotating the sound of Chinese characters and promoting Mandarin. It is not a phonetic script meant to replace Chinese characters." The sentence later became the official standard for the boundary between the Latin alphabet and Chinese characters.

On January 14, 2018, Google put Zhou Youguang on its homepage, marking a year since his death.

![A Google Doodle for Zhou Youguang](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180221154026YNioSbE7K9Xd8qzZ.jpeg-w600)

### 6. Why Do You Recognize So Many Characters You Can No Longer Write?

Wu Jun describes Chinese input's path from pinyin to shape and back to pinyin as "not a simple repetition, but a kind of sublimation."

It may not be as simple as sublimation.

Chinese people now learn characters through pinyin and type pinyin to make characters appear on screen, but in reading and handwriting the characters remain the only medium. Nobody can understand an article by reading its pinyin, and nobody uses pinyin to communicate in writing.

That looks like a compromise. People attached to traditional culture can take comfort that when it comes to writing, Chinese is still written in characters. For those convinced that Latinization brings us closer to a global culture, pinyin has done more than spare us a lot of trouble while we were learning characters; it has become an important part of how we think.

"Hand cancer" is now an internet buzzword for typing so fast with an input method that you send a message without noticing the wrong character in it.

Many people can still pick out a character's radicals and components, and some can guess how an unfamiliar character sounds. For most people, not knowing how to write a character but knowing how to say it means very good odds of finding it in an input method — and in that situation pinyin's role in learning characters is magnified. At the same time, people may care less and less about exactly how a given character is written.

The result: you recognize plenty of characters you can no longer write.

Typing 嬴政, the name of the first Qin emperor, is easy, but plenty of people never notice the difference between 赢, 嬴, 蠃 — and perhaps 蠃 as well. As for 饕餮, you may have long forgotten how to write them, but when they turn up you know they mean gluttony, you happen to know the sound, you type taotie, and there the characters are.

This Latinization is plainly incomplete, though. When a string like "zhi he bi z nide shh zho yj jians dao jiej yu wu，nide yuy ken yj js zg yzi l" appears, you are lost. Type it into a computer, though, and the input method may tell you what it says: "Paper and pen have shrunk to nearly nothing in your life; your language may already look exactly like this."

Many people know the next experience too: while writing, an input method's suggestions quietly change the words you choose, in a way pen and paper never do. Input methods offer more options, and those options were often not in the writer's mind to begin with.

In 2002 a team of scientists at Oxford studied whether pinyin and Chinese characters differ in how people process them. Scanning people's brains, they found clear differences in how strongly different regions fired when reading pinyin versus reading characters. From that they hypothesized that pinyin and characters set off different cognitive responses at the neurobiological level.

Wang Yongmin and Zhu Bangfu have both taken to tying Chinese characters to Chinese culture in recent years. In his *Qiushi* article, Wang Yongmin wrote: "Chinese characters are the root and bloodline of Chinese culture, the greatest cultural heritage of the Chinese nation. How could we throw them away and stop using them? The rise and fall of Chinese characters is every citizen's responsibility!"

To most ordinary people the argument seems more or less beside the point; apart from an occasional newspaper discussion of "forgetting how to write with a pen in hand," few worry about it. The people who once agitated for Latinization might find that most of their dream has come true.

A further question: when technology shifts again, will pinyin keep the place it holds now?

Globally, text still holds an irreplaceable position for information density, but images replacing text has been argued over for years. Yang Hongtao believes that if the shape of our devices changes — "becoming smartwatches, becoming smart glasses" — pinyin could go through another revolution.

Through all of it, the way language tools shape thinking will keep working on us.
